items.originalTitle: ‘Grandfather’ or ‘godfather’? Republicans know they’re stuck with Trump
items.author: Andrew Howard and Aaron Pellish
items.title: ‘Grandfather’ or ‘godfather’? Republicans know they’re stuck with Trump
items.summary: Republican leaders grappling with how to recover after their devastating midterm losses agree on one thing: President Donald Trump isn't going anywhere in 2028, even if some wish he would. Interviews with more than two dozen GOP state and county officials from red, blue and purple states across the country conducted since Election Day revealed a party still processing their election drubbing and at a loss for how to move forward. Some want to move on from Trump entirely. Some are eager for his involvement. And others are just resigned that he’s going to do whatever he wants, regardless of their preferences. All of them are worried about the party’s chances of retaining control of the White House in two short years, but they also recognize its current occupant is going to continue to exercise a huge role in the future of the party. “President Trump is going to be part of it, whether we want that or not,” said Arkansas GOP chair Joseph Wood. “His voters are still going to be Republicans that we need to have come out in this election in two years.” That leaves the party in a precarious position. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found the president’s approval rating at 32% overall, and at 70% among Republicans — down from 91% on inauguration day last year. A POLITICO Poll taken after the midterms found 56% of Trump’s 2024 voters believe the Republican Party needs to distance itself from him and his agenda. But no one in the party expects that to happen. And Trump has already taken steps to maintain his grip on the GOP, endorsing Republican National Committee Chair Joe Gruters for another term and ordering his powerful super PAC to continue fundraising ahead of 2028. A handful of Republican grassroots leaders were openly critical of Trump. “I don't know how much he really has to offer,” said Vermont GOP chair Paul Dame. “I think most people are ready to move on in a new direction.” Added Michael Bub, the chair of ruby-red Taylor County, Wisconsin, Republican Party :“He should stay out of it. Look at the people he endorsed: They lost.” In a statement, RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassare said “President Trump remains the unequivocal leader of our party.” “Republicans will continue to harness his ability to energize our voters and expose the Democrats' disastrous record to win in 2028,” she said. The White House demurred, pointing to the RNC’s response. Many party officials are resigned to Trump doing whatever he wants, given his domineering personality and strong sway over the party base. Nebraska Republican Party Chair Mary Jane Truemper said “Donald Trump's going to play whatever role he wants to play.” “He's the president,” Truemper said. “I look at things as they are and not as I want them to be.” That’s leaving some state-level Republican leaders wanting the president to take on a more constructive role and be willing to let other candidates and ideas rise. “I hope he becomes kind of the mentor grandfather, and not the godfather,” said Kansas GOP chair Danedri Herbert. “In America, we hope and expect our presidents to not keep a tight grip on the party, to recognize that now it's time for me to mentor the next generation.” Added outgoing Minnesota Republican Party Chair Alex Plechash: “We need to capitalize on what he brought to the party and do what we can to retain that. But there has been a definite turn in the political landscape.” Virtually every GOP official cited the poor political environment caused in part by the president’s handling of the economy and the war in Iran as the reason for the party’s midterm meltdown. But many stopped short of laying the blame directly at the president’s feet, a sign of how criticism of Trump is still verboten within the party. “I don't want to play the blame game, because I just don't think it's productive,” said West Virginia GOP chair Josh Holstein. “But I do think that it was more economics than it was anything.” Many GOP chairs praised the president’s ability to bring in new voters to the party and credited him for working to turn those voters out on behalf of other candidates. Still, some said they hope Trump’s generation-defining tenure at the top of the party comes to an end, allowing Republicans to choose the nominee without his influence. “Republicans should embrace whoever we decide we're going to get behind as a new president, and let the Trump era be gone by the time we're in 2028,” said Oklahoma GOP chair Charity Linch. Ben Proto, Connecticut’s GOP chair, said he is focused on what he and the RNC can control ahead of 2028 — and wants to make sure the organization stays neutral. “We shouldn't put our hand on the scale,” he said of the 2028 primaries. “I think Republican primary voters are pretty savvy and pretty smart and can figure out who our best candidate is going into the ’28 election.” Trump still has plenty of defenders. Even some chairs who are bucking Trump’s endorsement of Gruters and backing RNC co-chair KC Crosbie’s challenge to him, like Kentucky chair Robert Benvenuti, think Trump should continue to be heavily involved in 2028. “He won't take a back seat and should not take a back seat,” Benvenuti said. “I think he's been a tremendous leader for our country. … I think his message will still ring true and will be very helpful as we go into 2028.” Samuel Benson, Lauren Fedor and Jason Beeferman contributed to this report.

items.originalTitle: Amazon’s first digital photo frame is up to 50 percent off for Black Friday
items.author: Sheena Vasani
items.title: Amazon’s first digital photo frame is up to 50 percent off for Black Friday
items.summary: Amazon only announced its first digital photo frame less than a month ago, but it’s already getting a sizable discount for Black Friday. You can currently grab the Alexa Photo Frame at Amazon and Best Buy starting at $114 ($115 off), making it a great holiday gift for anyone who loves displaying family photos. If you prefer the walnut trim over the birch or standard black models, it’s also on sale at Best Buy for $134.99 ($95 off) — which, like with the others, is the first discount we’ve seen. Amazon Alexa Photo Frame Where to Buy: $229.99 $114.99 at Amazon (birch) $199.99 $114.99 at Best Buy (black) $229.99 $134.99 at Best Buy (walnut) The Alexa Photo Frame features a 10-inch, semi-matte touchscreen that’s designed to make digital photos look more natural, with built-in light sensors that automatically adjust brightness throughout the day. It displays images from Amazon Photos, which supports uploads from both iOS and Android devices, including photos stored in iCloud. You can choose which people or albums to display, or let Alexa Plus do the work, which often results in photos based on your facial expression, the season, and even the lighting. You can also search for specific photos with voice commands, letting you easily pull up images of your first dog, your child as a baby, and other shots without having to scroll endlessly through years of photos yourself. If you want to add a more personal touch, Amazon also lets you attach voice notes to individual photos via the Amazon Photos app. For example, you can add a recording of your kid explaining their Halloween costume to a trick-or-treating photo. Plus, you can preload the frame with photos and recordings before gifting it, so your loved one won’t have to spend time setting it up. We’re still testing Amazon’s answer to the Aura frame, but it looks like a particularly good option if you’re already an Amazon Prime member. A Prime subscription grants you unlimited full-resolution photo storage and access to Alexa Plus at no additional cost, and unlike Amazon’s smart displays, the frame doesn’t serve up annoying ads. That said, you don’t need a subscription to use it, and new users can always access a limited-time trial of Alexa Plus.
